problem: Robot spatial-semantic memories such as HLSM, FiLM and VLMaps are coarse, tied to a fixed class list or a 2D grid discretization, and need dense human annotation. Web-scale vision-language models like CLIP give rich open-vocabulary semantics but work only on single 2D images, with no 3D, multi-view-consistent integration.
motivation: Robots in homes need a queryable memory of where things are that accepts free-form language, such as 'warm up my lunch', without per-scene human labeling. Two observations drive the paper: neural implicit fields (Instant-NGP) are now fast enough to serve as differentiable spatial databases, and off-the-shelf web-trained models (Detic, CLIP, Sentence-BERT) can supply dense but noisy per-pixel labels. Fusing those labels into a 3D field should enforce multi-view consistency and denoise them.
key_idea: Train a per-scene neural field g(x,y,z) (Instant-NGP hash encoding plus MLP heads) with contrastive losses to regress Sentence-BERT label embeddings and CLIP visual embeddings. The labels come from back-projecting Detic/CLIP outputs on RGB-D frames, so 3D points become directly queryable by text or image embeddings.
insight: Fusing noisy 2D web-model predictions into one 3D field adds multi-view consistency that beats the teacher itself. In Fig. 6, CLIP-Fields trained only on zero-shot Detic labels achieves higher semantic-segmentation AP on HM3D Semantics than Detic does, and the gap grows with more labeled views. The 3D prior also makes the method very label-efficient: with only three annotated views it exceeds fine-tuned Mask-RCNN and DeepLabV3 (Fig. 5). Under synthetic label-flip noise, accuracy degrades roughly linearly with base-model accuracy rather than collapsing (Fig. 7). The flip side is that the field inherits systematic detector errors: a floor patch labeled 'table', or the dishwasher returned for 'wash my hand'.
method: Dataset creation: RGB-D frames with odometry (iPhone 13 Pro LiDAR, or HM3D renders) are back-projected to world point clouds. Each point is labeled with the Detic label and confidence (or GT annotation), the CLIP embedding of the Detic region (or frame) it came from, and its camera distance.
Trunk: an Instant-NGP multi-resolution hash encoding maps (x,y,z) to a 144-d vector (18 levels, per-level scale 2, level dim 8, log2 hashmap 20).

Heads: 2-layer ReLU MLPs (hidden 600). The semantic head f outputs 768-d, matching Sentence-BERT all-mpnet-base-v2 label embeddings. The visual head h outputs 512-d, matching CLIP ViT-B/32 embeddings. An optional instance-ID head outputs one-hot instance IDs when GT instances exist.

Losses: an InfoNCE-style semantic loss weighted by detector confidence, a visual loss weighted by exp(-camera distance), both with learned temperature, plus α=100 times cross-entropy for instance ID. Training uses a batch of 12,544 points, Adam with lr 1e-4, and 100 epochs of 3e6 iterations each, on one Quadro GP100.

Querying: text is encoded with Sentence-BERT (semantic part) and the CLIP text encoder (visual part). The system returns the 3D point maximizing the dot product with f/h. Image queries use the CLIP image embedding against h for view localization. Segmentation is obtained by back-projecting depth pixels and decoding per-point embeddings.
Robot execution: on a Hello Robot Stretch, Hector SLAM's classic navigation stack drives to the argmax point and the camera is pointed at that XYZ ('Go and look at X').

setting.backbone: Per-scene Instant-NGP hash-grid + MLP heads trained from scratch, supervised by frozen Detic (CLIP+SwinB), CLIP ViT-B/32 and Sentence-BERT all-mpnet-base-v2
setting.training_data: Per-scene only: RGB-D frames with camera poses of the target scene. Labels come either from few-shot GT HM3D-Semantics instance/semantic annotations (1-144 labeled images) or from zero-shot Detic predictions (ScanNet200 vocabulary on the robot scenes) plus CLIP embeddings. No human labels are used in the zero-shot and robot settings.
setting.observation: Pre-collected RGB-D frames with 6-DoF odometry (iPhone 13 Pro LiDAR in the real world); queries are text or images
setting.action_space: Target 3D point handed to the classic Hector SLAM navigation stack, then camera pointing at that XYZ
setting.simulator: HM3D Semantics (Habitat-Matterport 3D) renders for segmentation evaluation; real world for navigation
setting.privileged: The scene is pre-explored and pre-scanned (RGB-D with poses) before querying. For zero-shot segmentation, the per-scene semantic label list is given.

numbers_note: No numeric results tables. Segmentation results (low-shot instance mAP Fig. 4, low-shot semantic AP Fig. 5, zero-shot Detic vs CLIP-Fields AP Fig. 6, label-noise robustness Fig. 7) are given only as plots on a subset of HM3D Semantics scenes. Real-robot navigation used 20 queries in a kitchen and 15 in a library and is reported qualitatively. Only the kitchen per-query log (Appendix VII-B) is itemized, with success or failure per query, and no aggregate success rate is printed. The method is not evaluated on any standard navigation benchmark such as ObjectNav or VLN.
results: On HM3D Semantics, CLIP-Fields beats fine-tuned Mask-RCNN (ResNet50-FPN) and DeepLabV3 (ResNet50) at few-shot instance and semantic segmentation; with only three labeled views it already exceeds all RGB baselines in semantic AP (figures only). Trained purely on Detic labels, it outperforms zero-shot Detic itself across 6-144 labeled images. Its accuracy scales roughly linearly with simulated base-label accuracy. On a Stretch robot in two real scenes, it handles literal, visual and semantic language queries, including misspellings. Failures come from detector mislabels, confusion between related concepts, and over-weighting semantic matches in visual queries.
limitations: Per-scene training on a static, pre-scanned environment: no parameter sharing across scenes, no dynamic objects, and exploration is assumed already done.
Quality is bounded by the web detector's labels: misdetections propagate, and there are semantic confusions such as dishwasher vs sink.
Evaluation is small-scale: segmentation is shown only as plots on an HM3D subset, and robot navigation covers 35 qualitative 'look-at' queries with no standard nav benchmark or metrics.
